summary:
Smokeshed is a web app that turns more than 20 years of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent burning activity calendar for any place on Earth.
The fire record is split between MODIS (since 2000) and the sharper VIIRS (since 2012), which sees about 12 times as many fires, so the two can't be compared directly. We harmonized them: while both satellites flew (2013–2014), we measured the MODIS-to-VIIRS ratio in each 10° region and converted the older MODIS counts. Tested on a year it never saw, the conversion had an 11% median error.
Pick a place and Smokeshed answers in plain language: are fires in the last 7 days above normal? A month-by-month calendar from 2001 to today highlights unusual months and the usual fire season, with a long-term trend and a CSV download. For Singapore it adds a "smokeshed" early warning: in 2026, haze rose about one day after fires surged in Sumatra.
With the MODIS satellites shutting down, harmonizing now keeps two decades of fire history usable for responders, scientists and land managers.
details:
What it does

Smokeshed is a free web app that answers two questions for any place on Earth: Is it burning more than normal right now? and How has burning changed here since 2001?

  • Right now: fire detections from the last 7 days, compared with a normal week for this month, give a plain status: Quiet, Normal, Above normal or Surge. A "Coming up" line says whether next month is usually busier, so responders can plan ahead.
  • History: a month-by-month burning calendar from 2001 to today.
    • A "Usual" row shows a typical year, with the fire season marked.
    • A "Compared with normal" view turns unusual months red and quieter ones blue.
    • Yearly bars show the long-term trend.
    • A CSV download gives the monthly numbers.
  • Famous fires: one click on Indonesia 2015, Australia's Black Summer, the Pantanal 2020, California 2020 or Canada 2023 shows the summary and the months in the calendar.
  • Singapore's smokeshed: Singapore has almost no fires of its own, yet suffers haze from Sumatra and Kalimantan. For Singapore, Smokeshed shows these source regions and gives a haze warning based on how the city's air has responded to their fires, plus the live wind direction and Singapore's current PM2.5.

How it works

  1. Data: NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots: MODIS (Terra) 2001–2014 and VIIRS S-NPP 375 m 2013–2026, counted per month on a 1° grid (about 110 km). We keep vegetation fires only and drop low-confidence detections and known gas flares.
  2. Harmonization: VIIRS sees about 12× as many fires as MODIS, but the ratio varies by region, from 8× in California to 15–20× over Indonesian peatlands. While both satellites flew (2013–2014), we measured the ratio separately in each 10° region and converted older MODIS counts into VIIRS-equivalent counts.
    • We chose 2013–2014 because MODIS's orbit has drifted in recent years.
    • We used Terra only, because the Aqua satellite only started in mid-2002 and would have made 2001–02 look artificially quiet.
  3. Validation:
    • Ratios learned from 2013 alone predicted 2014 VIIRS totals with an 11% median error across 189 fire regions.
    • Without being told, the record shows Indonesia's El Niño haze years and the wet La Niña years, and each famous fire is the busiest month on record in its area.
  4. Right now: the last 7 days come from the FIRMS near-real-time feed, using the freshest VIIRS satellite. When we built this, that was NOAA-20, because S-NPP's feed had paused on 2 Nov 2026.
  5. Smokeshed test: we compared daily hotspots in Sumatra and Kalimantan with Singapore's daily PM2.5 (Jun–Nov 2026). Singapore's air got worse about 1 day after Sumatra's fires surged (r = 0.67). Kalimantan's link was weaker (r = 0.47, about 6 days). This matches the monsoon winds and a Harvard/Columbia study that found South Sumatra matters most for Singapore.
  6. Delivery: Python scripts pre-compute small JSON files, and a static website reads them, with no server, no login and no cost to run. A small script refreshes the last-7-days data, built to run daily as a GitHub Action. Live wind (Open-Meteo), Singapore's PM2.5 (data.gov.sg) and NASA GIBS satellite images load directly in the browser.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Emergency responders and early warning: a plain-language status, a "coming up" outlook, and for Singapore a haze warning that uses the live wind.
  • Scientists: one consistent 25-year record across sensors, honest uncertainty (converted months are marked ±11%) and a CSV download.
  • Land managers: each area's usual fire season, unusual years and long-term trend at a glance.
  • Urgency: the MODIS satellites begin shutting down from late 2026. Harmonizing now keeps two decades of fire history usable.

How it is creative

  • A new user group: most fire tools ask "what is burning here?". Smokeshed also asks "whose smoke am I breathing?", for people who live downwind of fires.
  • Bridging tools that never met: NASA FIRMS has the data, Global Forest Watch compares years, and Harvard's SMOKE Policy Tool models smoke. Smokeshed brings a harmonized record, a calendar compared with history, and the smoke link into one click.
  • Validation as a story: clicking a famous fire shows our harmonized record recognising it as the busiest month on record.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty:
    • Every number on the page is computed from the data.
    • We dropped famous fires that didn't stand out in fire counts.
    • Tiny month-to-month differences stay grey, so they don't look like alarms.
    • We say plainly that the smoke link is a correlation over one season.
  • Simplicity: one click gets an answer, every chart comes with a sentence in plain English, and an optional 30-second guided tour introduces the page.
  • Accessibility: colour-blind-safe palettes, labels that never rely on colour alone, a keyboard-friendly tour, and a layout that works on phones.
  • Security: the FIRMS API key is used only by the data scripts, never in the website.

Tools

Python (standard library, matplotlib), JavaScript, HTML and CSS (no framework), the Leaflet map library, GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions. We used Claude (Anthropic's AI assistant, via Claude Code) to help write code and documentation; commits it helped with are marked in our git history.

Limitations and next steps

The calendar uses 1° squares, and the smokeshed is shown for Singapore only. Next: smokesheds for more cities (Kuala Lumpur, Bangkok, Chiang Mai), a finer grid, smoke-direction forecasts and alerts.
